concept.name: Exchange inflow
concept.definition: Exchange inflow is the volume of coins transferred on-chain into wallets attributed to centralized exchanges over a period, watched as a leading indicator of intent to sell or trade.
concept.intuition: Coins moving onto an exchange are like goods carried into a pawnshop — they are positioned to be sold, even if the sale hasn't happened yet.
concept.mechanics: On-chain analytics firms (Glassnode, CryptoQuant) label exchange-controlled addresses and sum transfers into them; inflow is reported in native units or USD per day. Spikes historically cluster around sharp price moves — the March 2020 crash saw deposit volumes surge as holders rushed to sell — while deposit counts and average deposit size distinguish retail from whale behavior.
concept.failure_modes: Attribution depends on heuristics and labeled wallets, so new exchange addresses or internal reshuffles can masquerade as inflows; inflow ≠ immediate selling, since market makers and custodians also receive deposits for operational reasons.
concept.misconceptions: A large inflow is not a guaranteed dump — coins may sit on the exchange for months, and inflows can also fund derivatives collateral or market-making. Raw inflow without reserve context (is the total balance actually growing?) misleads.
concept.example: During the March 2020 crash, BTC exchange inflow spiked to unusually high volumes as panicked holders deposited to sell; Glassnode noted the number of daily deposits simultaneously hit a 3-year low, meaning the spike was driven by large whale-sized deposits.

citations.source: Glassnode Insights - The Number of BTC On Exchanges Is Down Almost 7%
